title: Colonial administration and the colonial states
competency: Compare British and French colonial policies and explain the political economy of colonial agriculture, mining and trade.

ideas.name: British indirect rule and French assimilation

en.text: Britain used indirect rule, worked out by Frederick Lugard in Northern Nigeria and described in The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa (1922): it ruled through African chiefs, cheaply, with few Europeans, and stressed "tribal" differences to divide and rule. France aimed to assimilate Africans through French language, law and citizenship, fully only in the Four Communes of Senegal, and Albert Sarraut laid the foundations of direct rule. Britain used traditional rulers and gave chiefs more power; France gave them less, and nine-tenths of schooling in French Africa was by the state, in French. Both systems made chiefs dependent on their colonial masters.

screens.title: Guess first: British or French?
screens.after: Britain ruled through chiefs; France tried to make Africans French. The rest of this idea explains why.

screens.title: British indirect rule
paras: Formulated most clearly by Frederick Lugard.
He worked it out in Northern Nigeria.
His book: The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa (1922).
Britain ruled through African chiefs.
It was the cheapest way to rule many people with few Europeans.
It varied a lot from colony to colony.
Britain stressed "tribal" differences: "divide and rule".
This made African unity harder.

screens.title: French assimilation and direct rule
paras: France wanted to make Africans French.
Tools: French language, French law, French rights.
Fully applied only in Senegal's Four Communes.
1848: they could elect a deputy to the National Assembly in Paris.
Elsewhere, only Africans who read, wrote and spoke French well could become citizens.
Albert Sarraut, Minister of Colonies (1920–24, 1932–33), founded "direct rule".

en.text: Belgium ruled the Congo, Rwanda and Burundi; its rule in the Congo rested on a "colonial trinity" of the state, missionaries and private companies. Portugal, in Angola and Mozambique, had no clear policy; its rule was mostly oppressive, with an assimilation policy that was never fully applied. Germany (1884–1914) used direct rule like France, with enough personnel to exploit the resources of Tanganyika as fully as possible.

en.text: Colonies were to supply raw materials and buy European goods, so colonial governments pushed Africans to grow cash crops: palm oil, palm kernels, groundnuts, cocoa, coffee and cotton. Chiefs often ran export plantations with unpaid forced labour, and cotton was usually grown only under compulsion. Groundnuts were the main crop of Senegal and northern Nigeria, cocoa of the Gold Coast and south-western Nigeria, coffee of Côte d'Ivoire, Uganda and Tanganyika. After the Great Depression prices fell while taxes stayed, so peasants planted more cash crops, food was neglected, soils were exhausted, and famine followed, as in Niger in 1931.

en.text: Mining was the colonial sector most profitable for investment. Colonial governments claimed all minerals and leased them to European companies. Britain took the gold fields of Asante; tin was dug open-cast on the Jos plateau in northern Nigeria with masses of unskilled labour. The richest area was the copper belt of Katanga (Union Minière) and Northern Rhodesia, fed by maize and cattle from white farmers and fuelled by Hwange coal from Southern Rhodesia, which also produced gold, copper and asbestos. Southern Africa's main mining centre was the Witwatersrand.

notes.text: p.43: the book's crop–country list is mixed up (groundnuts in Côte d'Ivoire, Angola, Tanganyika, Uganda; cocoa in northern Nigeria and Senegal; coffee in the Gold Coast). The lesson teaches the corrected pairs: groundnuts – Senegal, northern Nigeria; cocoa – Gold Coast, south-western Nigeria; coffee – Côte d'Ivoire, Angola, Tanganyika, Uganda, eastern Belgian Congo. Exams may copy the book's wording.
p.43: the irrigation scheme "between the Blue Nile and White Nile" is the Gezira Scheme in central Sudan, not "Southern Sudan" (the lesson names Gezira).

Spellings and misprints: "Luggard" = Lugard; "pirvate" = private; "graze" = grew; "failing real incomes" = falling; "open-caste" = open-cast; "Union Muniere" = Union Minière du Haut-Katanga; "Ubangui Chari" = Ubangi-Shari.

p.41: full assimilation applied only to the Four Communes of Senegal (Saint-Louis, Gorée, Rufisque, Dakar), not all Senegalese; they elected a deputy from 1848 but full citizenship was confirmed only in 1916.
